title: Master Class | Scandinavian Defense | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We're White against the Scandinavian: the pawn to e4, d5, we take on d5, and instead of recapturing with the queen Black plays the knight to f6.
The bishop to b5 with check — the line I like. It's just a matter of knowing the patterns.
Black blocks with the knight from b8 to d7.
Now —
the bishop to d7 is, I believe, the more popular block.
The idea is to drop the bishop back to e2.
After the knight takes d5, we play d4. Look how awkward Black's light-squared bishop is — in the way of everything.
So most of the time Black spends another move on it, the bishop to f5, and White keeps a slight edge.
The knight to f3.
Black plays e6. The position is tremendously solid, so if you want a solid, reputable line, this is worth considering.
There's a positional trap here: a lot of people play c4. Why is c4 less good than it looks — what's Black's annoying response?
The bishop to b4 with check isn't the answer — it doesn't do much.
White just blocks with the bishop to d2.
Black's bishop would hang, so Black takes on d2 —
— and White recaptures with the queen, in great shape. The point was the knight to b4, not the bishop.
It's the knight to b4, not the bishop to b4.
Why is the knight to b4 suddenly so strong? Because it's very hard to defend against the knight to c2 — a fork.
White's only serious defence to the knight to c2 is the knight to a3, and look how bad that knight is — it can't re-enter the game.
No disaster has happened, but White —
— has real developmental problems. With White's knight stranded and Black's so strong, Black is super active and can strike in the centre with c5.
That c5 break is annoying. So the way I like to play this with White —

— is the move a3 first, prophylaxis covering the square, and after the bishop retreats, c4, the capture on f6, the knight to c3 — a slight edge for White, though Black can analyze it close to equality; White's a touch better for more central control and active development.
That extra central control and development is the point. Anyway, Black went the knight from b8 to d7. Let me show why c4 isn't as good as it looks.
After c4 —
If White takes and Black recaptures with the knight, look carefully: Black has a lead in development, the d4-hole is horrific, and White's bishop can't reach an active square.
So this is excellent for Black. If you're going to play c4, instead play d4 and transpose —
— the pawn to d4 —
— into the Panov Attack of the Caro-Kann, which frequently arises by this move order.
Via the Caro-Kann order: c4, the knight to f6, the knight to c3.
So it's just a transposition where Black is considered totally fine by theory —

— but it's an interesting line. Now: the knight from b8 to d7, the knight to c3, a6, and refraining from the bishop to a4 and b5, Black plays the knight to b6, we go d4 — and here Black could take the queen, but the knight takes d5 is more solid, then the knight to f3. A great example of concrete thinking: I said c4 was bad in the other position, but you can't assume it's bad here and reflexively play a3 — you'd waste time. c4 is good here because the situation differs: before, a pawn stood at e6 protecting the knight; now the queen to a4 with check wins, since after the knight to c6, b5, and c takes b5. Think concretely.
